title: After a blue wave, Trump will dig in his heels. We must be more vigilant than ever | Steve Cohen and Michael Shank
text:
Americans just witnessed a blue tsunami in the midterm elections, with historic firsts across many US states: the country’s first female Black governor, first female Native American governor, first Muslim US senator, and more.
And while the voters’ repudiation of Donald Trump’s agenda is clear, as Democrats seize the majority of both chambers of Congress, the work to defend our institutions from further democratic backsliding won’t ease up overnight.
Vigilance is needed now more than ever as the Trump administration inevitably digs in its heels.
The White House has already mapped out its plan for the next two years to govern without Congress: more executive orders, actions and overreach, more vetoes, and more legal delays and obfuscation.
Not only will Republicans aim for retribution in a lame duck Congress, with one last reconciliation bill to enact their agenda without Democratic input, but we should expect the executive branch to lash out even more.
Don’t forget that this administration relentlessly sowed doubt about the legitimacy of the midterm elections, offered $1m for reports of voter fraud and $5,000 bribes tied to midterm results, fallaciously fearmongered about Chinese involvement in elections-tinkering, attempted to thwart mail-in voting and pressured US states to segregate ballots.
This democratic backsliding all happened in the last few weeks before the vote, and these anti-democratic behaviors won’t disappear quickly. Many expect they’ll escalate in the coming months, potentially under the fog of an escalated war on Iran, which is why vigilance is required in the months and years ahead.
State and local officials, who were preparing for worst-case scenarios in recent months, must not let down their guard.
In preparing local governments for additional attacks on democratic institutions, organizations such as the Mayors Innovation Project, and so many other democracy-defending institutions across the US, have been preparing local leaders with emergency management plans and protocols, with the stated caveat this is just a starting point to protect democracy far into the future.
Similarly, local communities who were on the frontlines of this fight and where much of the democracy defense work was and is happening, from Free DC and Defend 612 to the many rapid response networks that popped up in US cities, cannot rest easy. We need this local leadership now more than ever.
A recent report titled The American Crisis rightly points out that it’s local communities, first and foremost, that are the “central locus of control in stabilizing America’s democratic transition, as republican power has always ultimately remained with the people”. We couldn’t agree more.
The report goes on to state that the US Congress cannot leave local communities to fight alone, and that it must assert itself as the primary branch of the federal government and take seriously its oath to uphold the constitution by ensuring a successful democratic transition of power.
That oath will be tested come January. We trust the new Congress will meet that challenge, and not just with oversight hearings and proceedings to hold the White House accountable for past and present corruption.
Assuming January’s swearing-in goes smoothly, and there’s no escalation of war on Iran by the White House that leads to emergency declarations, power outages or martial law, the work required of all of us is much bigger than a single voting day or swearing-in ceremony.
We must now bolster subnational governance and infrastructure at the local level. That’s how we strengthen the democratic muscle memory across the whole of American society.
The myriad community-based and neighborhood-led networks emerging in response to government repression are establishing the new social infrastructure and human capital necessary for long-term defense of our democratic institutions.
Defend 612 in Minneapolis, for example, now has an 80,000-strong network of concerned and activated individuals ready to rally in defense of democracy. Free DC, in Washington DC, has thousands of well-trained members ready to defend our nation’s great capital from further federal overreach, military occupation and more.
These groups will inevitably evolve to meet the democratic needs of the day, but this newly revitalized social infrastructure and human capital will be an essential complement and accountability check going forward.
These are welcome developments. And the new Congress will do well to work with these local movements, as our democratic infrastructure will only be as strong as the sinew we string between local, state and federal leaderships.
Americans want to be a part of something great; that’s without question. And ideally that something great is a healthy, thriving democracy. But when that is challenged, don’t be surprised to see Americans dig in locally to defend that which they love, their communities, their neighborhoods and their homes.
What we’re witnessing across this country is a powerful resurgence of democratic engagement and it’s just the beginning.
At 250 years old, perhaps we’re in fact experiencing a rebirth. Sure, it took a serious threat to realize what’s at stake, but the masses mobilizing have never been mightier. And it’s this very momentum that may save us.
- Congressman Steve Cohen is a fourth-generation Memphian who has served the ninth district of Tennessee since 2006
- Dr Michael Shank is adjunct professor at New York University’s Center for Global Affairs and George Mason University’s Carter School for Peace and Conflict Resolution
